newsitem.title: USA: Mass. expected to pass "Lizzie's Law" by July 15.
newsitem.headline: Mass. expected to pass "Lizzie's Law" by July 15.

text.p: Massachusetts was expected this month to become the first state to enact a measure that would prohibit judges from requiring children to visit a parent who has killed the other parent, officials said Thursday.

Known as "Lizzie's Law" after the 3-year-old who witnessed the murder of her mother at her father's hands, the bill was expected to be on Gov. William Weld's desk before the Legislature recesses on July 15.
It gives children like Lizzie Thompson, now 5, the right to refuse to visit a parent who has murdered the other parent.

Her father, Charles Thompson, is serving a life sentence without parole for the Aug. 3, 1995, murder of Andrea "Holly" Thompson. Despite a restraining order, he broke in through an upstairs window and stabbed his wife 24 times.
He then picked up Lizzie and placed her in her dead mother's arms. She remained with her mother's body for four hours before they were found.
Thompson, who was sentenced in May 1996, wrote to Lizzie's grandparents demanding she visit him in jail twice a month.

"Lizzie Thompson doesn't acknowledge him as her parent. She doesn't call him her dad. She doesn't call him her father. She just calls him 'the bad man that murdered Mommy,'" state Representative Paul Caron, the bill's sponsor, said in a telephone interview on Thursday.

The point of the measure "is to protect the child and the family of the victim," he said, adding that Thompson's behaviour was the "classic mode of operation of someone who's a domestic abuser. It's an attempt to exert control on the family once again.
"Reaching from behind the prison walls he succeeded in grabbing control of this family and forcing them to relive the horror of Holly's murder all over again."

Caron said the Massachusetts House and Senate were expected to pass the measure on July 14 so it can be on Weld's desk in time for the summer recess. He said he had received calls from legislators in Florida, Ohio, New Jersey and Texas looking to pass similar measures.
